skin-whitening-bleaching.summary: Lightening skin tone with topical agents, supplements or injections to fade dark spots and even out your complexion; long practiced worldwide, with documented risks from some products.

quick.overview:
Skin whitening, also called lightening or bleaching, uses chemical agents to reduce melanin so skin looks lighter and more even. People use it to fade dark spots, brighten the complexion and lift overall tone, and some looksmaxxing posters say it raises their rating by roughly 0.5 to 1 PSL.

Most lightening agents inhibit tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production; others block melanin transfer to skin cells or destroy melanocytes. Glutathione is reported to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin toward its lighter form. Agents such as hydroquinone, arbutin and kojic acid have been studied for pigmentation disorders, and the practice itself dates back more than two thousand years.
quick.how: People use topical creams and serums, oral supplements, or clinic-administered injections, usually as a routine over weeks to months, often alongside sunscreen and general skincare. Results show gradually as existing pigment fades and new pigment production is reduced.
quick.risks: Reported harms include mercury toxicity from contaminated products, skin thinning from long-term steroid creams, ochronosis and contact dermatitis from hydroquinone, and serious reactions from intravenous glutathione. Skin becomes more sun-sensitive. Many products are restricted or banned in several countries, and regulators and dermatology reviews document these problems.

angle.text: Users apply or take lightening agents to reduce melanin, fading dark spots and lifting overall skin tone for a brighter, more even complexion. Some forum posters say it raises their rating by about 0.5 to 1 PSL. Topical agents such as hydroquinone and arbutin have been studied clinically for pigmentation.

pheromone-cologne.summary: Fragrances sold with added pheromones to make the wearer more attractive to others; reviewers report no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior.

quick.overview:
Pheromone colognes are fragrances or sprays marketed as containing human sex pheromones, with the promise of a more appealing presence and more attention from others. Buyers wear them as a scent-based add-on to grooming and presentation.

The idea draws on research into compounds such as androstenone and androstadienone, which come from sweat glands and are proposed to act through the vomeronasal organ or olfactory receptors. A widely cited encyclopedia summary says no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and the human vomeronasal organ is described as vestigial in adults.
quick.how: People wear them like any cologne or body spray, applied after showering and usually alongside regular grooming and a normal fragrance routine. Any effect users notice is typically judged by how others react in social settings.
quick.risks: Reported direct risks are those of any fragrance product, such as skin irritation or allergy in some users. Reviewers note that the attraction effect advertised by sellers is not demonstrated in peer-reviewed work.

angle.text: Buyers wear these scents hoping the added pheromones make them more attractive and give them a more appealing presence, as a fragrance add-on to grooming. Reviewers report that no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior in a peer-reviewed study.

frenotomy-tongue-tie-release-for-face.summary: A short procedure releasing the tongue's frenulum, discussed online as a route to better tongue posture and a more defined jaw; studies cover feeding and speech, not facial appearance.

quick.overview:
A frenotomy or frenectomy releases the band of tissue under the tongue in people with tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a way to let the tongue rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth.

The procedure cuts or reshapes the lingual frenulum, sometimes with a laser, to increase tongue mobility. Published research examines breastfeeding, speech and sleep outcomes; no study found tests it for changing facial structure in children or adults. The link to palate and jaw development is presented as a hypothesis.
quick.how: It is done as a brief clinic procedure, often followed by tongue exercises or myofunctional therapy, and people combine it with practicing tongue posture and nasal breathing. Users in these communities describe judging results over months.
quick.risks: Reviews describe the procedure as simple with low complication rates in infants, but case reports and a systematic review document major complications after tongue-tie release. Experts disagree about how often tongue-tie causes problems and about diagnosis, particularly of posterior tongue-tie.

angle.text: Forum posters discuss releasing the tongue frenulum so the tongue can rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth. Studies cover feeding and speech outcomes rather than facial appearance.

face-rating-apps-ai-scoring.summary: Apps and AI tools that score a face photo for attractiveness so you can track changes like haircuts, grooming or angles over time.

quick.overview:
Face rating apps use algorithms to give a photo a numeric attractiveness score or tier, often on scales borrowed from looksmaxxing such as PSL. People use them to see how a haircut, grooming change, photo angle or other improvement shifts their number.

These tools typically assess features such as facial symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles and estimated age, and sometimes resemblance to reference faces. A well-known early example, the 2016 Beauty.AI contest, judged more than 60,000 entrants; 37 of its 44 winners were white, which critics cited as bias and the company attributed partly to limited data. No validation study of the individual apps was found.
quick.how: Users upload a front-facing photo, read the score, then retake photos after changes and compare. Many pair it with forum ratings and creator analyses, and keep lighting and angle consistent so the comparisons mean something.
quick.risks: Scores are model outputs that differ between apps and are not clinical measures. Reported concerns include bias from training data and the effect of numeric scoring on self-image; commentators link the wider looksmaxxing culture to body dysmorphia.

angle.text: Users submit photos to apps and AI tools for an attractiveness number or tier, then track it across haircuts, grooming changes and angles to see what moves it. Some convert the result to PSL. Scores are model outputs, and how well they track real-world appeal is largely unstudied.

psl-scale.summary: The community's 1-to-8 rating scale for male facial attractiveness, used as a shared yardstick for tracking progress from skin, hair or leanness changes.

quick.overview:
PSL, short for Perceived Sexual Levels, is an informal scale looksmaxxing communities use to rate male faces, usually from 1 to 8. It gives members a common benchmark and a target to aim for when they change skin, hair, leanness or style.

It sets out tiers from below average through normie and Chadlite up to Chad and beyond. Raters judge faces on features grouped under harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features. Its name is said to combine three forums where it arose, and no published study has evaluated the scale itself.
quick.how: People post photos for ratings, note their tier, then repost after changes such as a haircut, clearer skin or fat loss to see how opinions shift. Because raters differ, many collect several opinions.
quick.risks: The scale carries no physical risk. It is subjective and not scientifically validated, and commentators cited by Wikipedia link the surrounding culture of tiering people to body dysmorphia and distress.

angle.text: Community members use the PSL scale as a shared yardstick to rate male faces and to measure progress from changes such as skin, hair or leanness. The rating gives a concrete target to work toward, and it reflects community opinion rather than a validated measure.

canthal-tilt-theory.summary: The idea that a higher outer eye corner makes eyes look sharper and more attractive; the angle is measurable, and people use makeup, styling or procedures to change how it reads.

quick.overview:
Canthal tilt is the angle of the line joining the inner and outer eye corners relative to horizontal. In looksmaxxing, a positive tilt (outer corner higher) is read as sharper, more alert and more masculine, and many users aim for that look.

Tilt is set by the position of the eye corners, which are anchored by the canthal tendons and the shape of the bony orbit. Surgeons and researchers measure it routinely, and studies of pageant winners and attractiveness have reported tilt values, but no large trial establishes it as a principal driver of attractiveness. Makeup and lash styling change how tilt appears without altering anatomy.
quick.how: Most people start by measuring tilt from a straight-on photo, then use eyeliner, lash styling, brow shaping or hairstyle to change the impression. Some discuss posture, midface support or surgical options such as canthoplasty, which clinicians perform on the outer corner.
quick.risks: Measuring tilt carries no risk. Canthoplasty, canthopexy, filler and orbital or midface surgery are medical procedures with ordinary surgical risks, and some forum do-it-yourself approaches are ones clinicians would not endorse. Community threads also link the concept to distress for users who see a negative tilt as decisive.

angle.text: Forum users measure the angle of the eye corners and treat a positive tilt as a marker of a sharper, more attractive eye area, with makeup, styling or surgery used to change how it reads. The tilt itself is measurable; the strong rule built on it has had little direct testing.

hunter-eyes.summary: A looksmaxxing label for deep-set, slightly hooded eyes with an upward tilt and low brows, prized for an intense, masculine gaze.

quick.overview:
Hunter eyes describes an eye area that looks intense and masculine: deep-set, slightly hooded, with a positive canthal tilt, little visible white below the iris and low-set brows. It is contrasted with so-called prey eyes that are rounder, show more white and tilt downward.

Users attribute the look to bone structure such as orbit shape, brow ridge and cheekbone support, plus soft-tissue factors like lid hooding. The term has no formal definition in ophthalmology or anthropology, and no study has tested it as a category.
quick.how: People approximate the look with grooming and makeup, such as brow shaping, eyeliner and lash styling, and by lowering body fat to show the orbital area. Some try squinting or exercises, though users disagree on whether those change anything; surgical options discussed include canthoplasty, upper blepharoplasty and orbital procedures.
quick.risks: The concept itself carries no direct risk. Surgical and filler procedures talked about for the look carry standard risks such as asymmetry, dry eye, vision-related complications and revision surgery. Some critics link the trend to appearance anxiety.

angle.text: Hunter eyes are described online as an ideal eye area: a positive tilt, deep set and low brows that give an intense, masculine gaze. Users approximate it with grooming and makeup, and some try squinting or exercises. The term has no formal medical definition.

facial-width-to-height-ratio-fwhr.summary: Cheekbone width divided by upper-face height, used by forums as a masculinity score; research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression.

quick.overview:
FWHR is the width of the face across the cheekbones divided by the height from upper lip to brow. Looksmaxxing users measure it from photos and treat a wider value as a stronger, more masculine and imposing face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it.

Researchers have studied it since the late 2000s as a cue of dominance and aggression. A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio larger in men than women with a small effect (d = 0.11), and another found a small positive link with men's aggression; some studies have not replicated this, and scientific work often links higher values with perceived threat. A study of adolescents found no association with testosterone levels.
quick.how: People measure FWHR from a straight-on photo and compare it with community targets. They then adjust what they can, such as facial hair, hairstyle and leanness, which change how wide or narrow the face reads.
quick.risks: Measuring is harmless, though camera distance and lens change the measured value. Cosmetic or hormonal approaches to widen the face, including among minors, are medical interventions, and no study shows that treatments change FWHR.

angle.text: Forum users calculate fWHR from photos and treat a higher ratio as a sign of a stronger, more masculine face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it. Research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression.

golden-ratio-face-analysis.summary: Measuring your face against phi (about 1.618) and other ideal ratios to decide which features to improve; research finds little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness.

quick.overview:
Golden ratio face analysis compares facial measurements, such as mouth-to-nose width, eye spacing and facial thirds, with ideal ratios, most famously phi at about 1.618. Forum posters use the results to see which features sit close to the ideal and which to work on.

The underlying theory is that proportions near mathematical ideals read as harmonious and beautiful. A study of 286 young adults in Malaysia, summarized on Wikipedia, found no significant association between the golden ratio and attractiveness, and many claimed examples in art are disputed. The ratio targets used in looksmaxxing are informal community standards.
quick.how: People take a straight-on and a side photo, mark landmarks, calculate ratios and compare them to target values. They then use grooming, hairstyle, facial hair or other changes to shift how those proportions read.
quick.risks: The analysis is harmless, but critics link the practice and its numeric scoring of faces to appearance anxiety and body dysmorphia. The ratio targets are not validated for surgical planning.

angle.text: Forum posters measure features such as eye spacing and mouth-to-nose width against phi and other ideal ratios to decide which features to change. Studies have found little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness.

mogging-amog.summary: Looksmaxxing slang for outshining another man in looks, height, frame or voice; a social-comparison concept that frames improvement goals.

quick.overview:
To mog someone is to outclass them in looks or in a specific trait so they appear less attractive by comparison. The word is generally said to come from AMOG, short for alpha male of the group. For looksmaxxers it frames what to improve: face, height, body frame or voice.

It is a subculture concept rather than a scientific term, and no published study tests it directly. It rests on the idea that attractiveness is judged relatively, so standing next to a more attractive or taller man changes how you are perceived. Research on social comparison and contrast effects exists more broadly.
quick.how: People use the term to size up a room, a photo or a pairing, then pick goals such as gaining height, building a frame, improving the face or refining style so they come out ahead in comparisons.
quick.risks: Using the word carries no physical risk. Community threads and commentators link the culture around it with appearance anxiety, body dysmorphia and distress, and many posts frame ordinary encounters as contests.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use mogging as slang for outshining another man in a given setting, and it turns vague goals into specific ones such as more height, a sharper jaw or better style. It is a social concept drawn from anecdote, with no research of its own.

black-pill-ideology.summary: The incel-originated belief that genetics and looks largely fix a man's outcomes; researchers have studied it for links to mental-health burden and extremism.

quick.overview:
The black pill is a worldview from online incel forums holding that dating and social success are set largely by physical traits such as height and facial structure. In looksmaxxing it is discussed as the pessimistic counterpart to improvement-focused approaches: some users take it as motivation to optimize their looks, others as a source of despair, and some reject it as fatalistic.

The belief rests on claims about evolved mate preferences and selected dating-site statistics. Academic work studies it within research on incels, misogynistic extremism and mental health, for example a 2021 analysis of 9,062 forum comments and a 2024 study linking identity fusion with the incel ingroup to endorsement of violence against women.
quick.how: It is not a practice but a way of thinking. People engage with it by reading and posting in forums, and looksmaxxers who engage often argue over whether it pushes people to improve or to give up.
quick.risks: Research on incel communities reports high rates of depression, suicidality and social isolation among members, and a minority endorsement of violence against women; a 2022 survey cited by Wikipedia found most self-identified incels rejected violence. Anyone in distress can contact local crisis services.

angle.text: The black pill is a belief from incel communities that genetics and looks largely fix a man's outcomes, and looksmaxxing forums discuss it as the pessimistic counterpart to improvement-focused approaches. Researchers have studied it for links to mental-health burden and misogynistic extremism rather than for effects on appearance.

halo-effect.summary: The documented bias where one good trait, usually looks, makes people judge you as more capable, likable and trustworthy; the reason appearance gains pay off beyond looks.

quick.overview:
The halo effect is a cognitive bias in which a positive impression in one area, such as physical attractiveness, leads people to rate you more favorably on unrelated traits like intelligence, trustworthiness and competence. For looksmaxxers it is the reason better looks can mean more credibility, leniency and opportunity in school, work and dating.

The term goes back to Edward Thorndike's 1920 paper on ratings, and the attractiveness version was popularized by a 1972 study in which students rated attractive people as more socially desirable. Later work has examined it in essay grading, mock juries, voting and trust games. Researchers describe it as a general-impression effect, and the opposite pattern is called the horn effect.
quick.how: It is not something you do. People use it as a reason to invest in visible, first-impression traits such as grooming, skin, hair, style and fitness, since those change the impression others form before anything else is known.
quick.risks: It is a perception bias with no side effects of its own. Effect sizes vary by trait, target sex, culture and setting, and the bias can reverse; for example, attractive defendants were punished more harshly in a mock swindle case.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers cite the halo effect as the reason appearance gains pay off beyond looks: a good first impression leads others to judge you as more competent, likable and trustworthy. The effect is well documented in psychology, and its size varies by setting.

sexual-market-value-smv.summary: A manosphere and looksmaxxing term for your overall desirability as a partner, used to decide which improvements to prioritise; related to academic mate-value ideas.

quick.overview:
Sexual market value (SMV) is slang for how desirable someone is as a sexual or romantic partner, treated as a score in a dating marketplace. In looksmaxxing it is the goal that appearance improvements are said to raise, so users rank skin, hair, fitness and style by how much they might add.

SMV is described as a mix of facial attractiveness, height, body, status and money. Academics do not use the term, but they study related ideas such as sexual or erotic capital, mate value, the pay premium for attractiveness and the matching hypothesis. The community's specific weightings have not been tested.
quick.how: People use it as a framework for ranking themselves and others, often with decile scales or PSL, then pick the cheapest high-impact changes first, such as grooming, hairstyle, fitness and clothing.
quick.risks: No validated instrument measures SMV, and critics of related academic theories argue they overstate individual ownership of attractiveness and overlook culture, class and race. Community discussion includes race-based tier lists that scholars of sexual racism describe as reflecting bias in dating markets.

angle.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing users treat SMV as a total desirability score, with looks as one part, and use it to prioritise changes such as skin, hair, fitness and style that they expect to bring more attention from potential partners. It is a community term loosely related to academic mate-value research.

jestermaxxing.summary: Forum slang for using humor and playful behavior to be liked and remembered when looks alone aren't enough; research on humor and attraction exists, but not on the term.

quick.overview:
Jestermaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for relying on humor, banter and entertainment value to gain social standing and romantic interest, often as a complement to appearance. Members describe it as a way to be more likable and memorable, especially when they rate lower on looks.

Research on humor and mate choice exists and is mixed: humor is often rated as a desirable trait in partners, and one study reported funny men were rated more desirable for serious relationships only when also physically attractive. No dedicated research covers the term itself.
quick.how: People practice joking, banter and playful social behavior in group settings, usually alongside other improvements to looks and style. Proponents describe it as building personality and entertainment value; critics in the same forums say it fails if it comes across as desperate or fake.
quick.risks: No clinical risks are documented. Forum members describe social downsides such as being seen as the clown, regret about having played that role as a teenager, or a sense that it does not work without looks.

angle.text: Forum users describe leaning on humor and playful behavior to be more likable and memorable, and to win social and romantic attention as a complement to looks. Research exists on humor and attraction generally, with context-dependent results.

looksmatching.summary: Forum term for couples paired at a similar attractiveness level, the community version of the psychology matching hypothesis, which has real but mixed support.

quick.overview:
Looksmatching is looksmaxxing slang for couples in which both partners are about equally attractive. People use it to calibrate who they can expect to attract, and to set dating goals as they improve their looks.

It lines up with the matching hypothesis, proposed by Elaine Hatfield (then Walster) and colleagues in 1966, which holds that people tend to form relationships with partners of similar social desirability. Research finds support in couples and online-dating data, alongside criticism of its methods and explanations; critics suggest fear of rejection, proximity or shared status may drive the pattern.
quick.how: The term is used descriptively, for example when a poster notes that most couples at a gathering were looksmatches. People use it as a rough guide: as their own appearance improves, they expect to match with partners at a higher level.
quick.risks: No clinical risks apply. Reviewers note that attractiveness ratings are noisy and that research mostly uses student samples, so effect sizes are uncertain.

angle.text: Forum users use looksmatching to describe couples rated at a similar attractiveness level, and to calibrate who they can expect to attract once they improve. It parallels the psychology matching hypothesis, which has real but mixed support.

norwood-scale.summary: The standard seven-stage chart for grading male pattern hair loss, used to place your hairline and choose treatment, a transplant, hair systems or a buzz cut.

quick.overview:
The Norwood scale (Hamilton-Norwood) grades male pattern hair loss in seven stages, from a full head of hair at stage 1 to a narrow band of hair around the sides and back at stage 7. Placing your hairline on it helps you decide when to start treatment, whether a transplant makes sense, or whether a cropped or buzzed look suits you best.

It builds on James B. Hamilton's 1951 work and a 1975 revision by dermatologist O'Tar Norwood after studying 1,000 patients, which added the A variants for frontal recession. Dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons use it to describe severity and monitor change, and trials use it to define who is included.
quick.how: People compare photos of their hairline and crown against the chart, track their stage over time, and match treatments or styles to it. Looksmaxxing forums use stage numbers as shared shorthand, from NW0 hairlines to baldmaxxing at later stages.
quick.risks: The scale itself carries no risk. It is a visual classification, and reviewers report variable agreement between raters, limited fit for non-white populations, no information on how fast loss will progress, and a risk of self-misstaging, for example when judging wet hair.

angle.text: Users place their hairline on the seven-stage Norwood chart to size up male pattern hair loss and choose among treatments, transplants, hair systems or a buzz cut. It is the standard clinical classification used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons.

facial-symmetry-theory.summary: The idea that more symmetrical faces are more attractive and look healthier; studies find a real but modest, context-dependent link.

quick.overview:
Facial symmetry theory holds that faces with closely matching left and right sides look more attractive and healthier. Looksmaxxers use it as a guide for what to even out first, through grooming, hairstyle and posture, and in some cases fillers or surgery.

Research since the 1990s, including Grammer and Thornhill (1994), reports that symmetrical faces tend to get higher attractiveness ratings, independently of averageness. Later work found the effect for both sexes, stronger for female faces. The picture is mixed: effects differ by rating method, and some researchers argue symmetry matters mainly because it makes a face look typical. Links to objective health are described as inconsistent.
quick.how: People check symmetry in front-facing photos or mirror-flipped images, then work on what they can: hair parting, brow shaping, beard shaping, sleeping and chewing habits, posture. Forum guides also discuss fillers, implants and bone-related methods, and the effect of posture or non-surgical methods is untested.
quick.risks: The theory carries no direct risk. Clinical literature notes that marked asymmetry from conditions such as facial palsy or craniofacial microsomia affects quality of life and is treated medically or surgically. Community guides on correcting symmetry include procedures with their own medical risks.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use symmetry as a guide for what to even out first, so the face reads as more balanced and healthy, trying grooming, fillers, implants or posture work. Studies find a real but modest link between symmetry and attractiveness.

dimorphism-theory.summary: The idea that more sex-typical facial features, such as a strong jaw in men, raise attractiveness; research on it is real but mixed.

quick.overview:
Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framing that faces differ between the sexes in measurable ways, and that more strongly sex-typical features are more attractive: a pronounced jaw and brow and defined cheekbones in men, softer, more youthful features in women. Users apply it to choose beards, fat loss, haircuts and sometimes procedures that sharpen masculine features.

Proponents point to hormones, especially testosterone during puberty, shaping facial bone and soft tissue, with observers reading the features as signals of health. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness exists and is mixed: preferences for masculine male faces shift with factors such as menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, relationship status and country, and some studies find little link once perceived health is accounted for.
quick.how: People use it as a checklist for what to emphasize: lower body fat to show jaw and cheekbones, a beard to add jaw definition, and hairstyles that frame the brow. Some look into hormonal or surgical routes, which are covered in separate entries.
quick.risks: The theory itself is a descriptive framework with no direct risk. Hormone use or surgery to change facial structure carry their own medical risks.

angle.text: Forum users treat masculine features such as a strong jaw and defined cheekbones as central to male attractiveness, and use the idea to choose beards, fat loss or procedures that emphasize them. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness is real but mixed.

ascension.summary: Community term for a large improvement in your looks over time, usually documented with before-and-after photos; it names the outcome rather than a method.

quick.overview:
In looksmaxxing slang, ascension means a marked rise in perceived attractiveness, and to ascend is to undertake one. Members post plans, protocols and progress updates with before-and-after photos on looksmax.org, and the word is used for gains reached through changes like body-fat loss, skin, hair and style.

The term is a label for an outcome, so there is no single treatment or study behind it. Members describe combining several changes at once, depending on their plan, and some describe strong emotional reactions to looking better.
quick.how: People set a plan, usually combining changes such as fat loss, skincare, haircut and grooming, fitness, and in some cases dental or surgical work or hormones, then document progress with consistent photos over months.
quick.risks: Risks depend entirely on the methods used, and some methods carry documented medical risks covered in their own entries. Some forum posts note that ascension does not cure psychological issues.

angle.text: Ascension is the community word for a big improvement in looks over time, built from steps such as fat loss, skin, hair and style, with before-and-after photos documenting progress. It names an outcome rather than a method, and the results shown are individual self-reports.

hairstyle-maxxing.summary: Choosing a cut and style to suit your face shape and hair type; cheap and reversible, and the change shows as soon as the haircut is done.

quick.overview:
Hairstyle maxxing is picking a haircut and styling to suit your face shape, forehead size, head shape and hair type. The payoff is visible right after the cut: hair adds volume and texture, frames the face and hairline, and changes how much forehead and eye area shows.

Research in person perception treats hairstyle, clothing and makeup as part of first impressions, and a 2023 review argues dress, including hairstyle, belongs in models of how people judge one another. No trial has tested face-shape-matching rules as such.
quick.how: People bring reference photos to a barber or stylist and adjust length, volume, fringe and parting to their face and growth pattern. Many add styling products, and some use chemical straightening or waving. Forums are full of photo threads asking for hairstyle suggestions.
quick.risks: Haircuts are reversible and grow out. Dermatology reviews report that tight, tension-heavy styles can cause traction alopecia, and chemical straightening or waving carries its own review literature.

angle.text: Users pick a cut and styling to suit face shape, forehead size and hair type, and the change is visible as soon as the haircut is done. Research shows hair shapes first impressions.
